scenes.title: The Slide Rule Guide
scenes.subtitle: If, when, and how to use generative AI tools for education
scenes.byline: Ideas from an essay by Michael Heroux
scenes.narration: Hi, I'm Mike Heroux. This is The Slide Rule Guide: some ideas for if, when, and how to use generative AI tools in education.

scenes.heading: A familiar analogy

items.title: Calculator
items.body: Then use the tool to solve problems

scenes.narration: We often compare paper and pencil to the calculator. We want students to learn arithmetic by hand first. Then they use a calculator as a tool for solving real problems.

scenes.heading: Now add a third item

lines.text: For three centuries, the best calculating tool there was.
Then, in the 1970s, calculators arrived. Within a few years it was gone.

scenes.narration: I want to add a third item: the slide rule. For more than three centuries, it was the best calculating tool available. Then, in the 1970s, calculators arrived, and within a few years the slide rule was gone.

lines.text: They make some — but not all — of our teaching and learning approaches
the equivalent of a slide rule.
lines.cue: the equivalent of a slide rule

scenes.narration: I believe generative AI tools are the new calculators. They make some, but not all, of our approaches to teaching and learning the equivalent of a slide rule.

scenes.heading: The educator's job: choose the right tool

items.title: Calculator
items.body: when the tool serves the learning

footer.text: Like paper and pencil, or like a calculator — but not like a slide rule.

scenes.narration: Our challenge as educators is to make our approaches like paper and pencil when students need to build foundational skills. They should be like a calculator when the tool serves the learning, but never like a slide rule.

scenes.heading: What does “slide rule” work look like?

items.text: Manually summarizing large bodies of text

footer.text: Required not because the process was valuable,
but because there was no faster way to get the result.

scenes.narration: Many of our assignments, such as summarizing large bodies of text, writing repetitive code, or composing boilerplate reports, were required because there was no faster way to get the result. The process itself was not what mattered.

scenes.heading: Two risks for educators

items.title: Permitting too much
items.body: Allowing AI as a calculator when paper and pencil is required
items.result: Students miss fundamentals they need for life after college

items.title: Prohibiting too much
items.body: Banning AI where it would accelerate learning and productivity
items.result: Students get a slide rule when they need a calculator
items.result_cue: we hand students a slide rule

scenes.narration: In my experience, we run two risks. First, we permit these tools when students need paper and pencil, and they miss the fundamentals. Second, we prohibit them when they would accelerate learning, and we hand students a slide rule when they need a calculator.

scenes.heading: The real challenge

left.title: Exercises that build essential understanding
left.body: Like learning arithmetic by hand. Keep them.

right.title: Obsolete workflows
right.body: Replace or enhance them by focusing students on what they do with AI output:

scenes.narration: So the real work is to tell the difference. We should keep the exercises that build essential understanding. For the obsolete workflows, we should redirect students toward interpretation, creativity, and critical thinking about what the AI produces.

scenes.footer: Read the essay: maherou.github.io  ·  “The Slide Rule Guide” (Heroux, 2025)
scenes.narration: Pencil when it builds. Calculator when it serves. Never a slide rule.
